slides.title: Building Sentences
slides.subtitle: Lesson 10 · Simple, Compound & Complex · the Interjection

slides.text: A Simple Sentence consists of a single proposition.
examples: Ellen and Mary study botany.  (compound subject — still one proposition)

slides.heading: Combining Sentences
bullets: “I see a dog.”  “I see a boy.”  “I see a tree.”  “I see a house.” — *I see* is a part common to all of them.
Use the common part but once, and the four become a single sentence:  “I see a dog, a boy, a tree, and a house.”

slides.heading: Practice — Combining (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Combine the sentences in each group into a single sentence.
items: I found a book. I found a pencil. I found a slate. I found a knife.
John walked to the lake. John walked over the hill. John walked rapidly.
The horse was old. The horse was lame. The horse was blind.
answers: I found a book, a pencil, a slate, and a knife.
John walked rapidly over the hill to the lake.
The horse was old, lame, and blind.

slides.heading: Practice — Combining (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Combine the sentences in each group into a single sentence.
items: Apple trees grow thriftily. Apple trees grow in our orchard.
The wind blew fiercely. The wind blew last night. The wind blew from the north.
William gave me a new book. William sold me ten marbles. William bought a sled for my brother.
answers: Apple trees grow thriftily in our orchard.
The wind blew fiercely from the north last night.
William gave me a new book, sold me ten marbles, and bought a sled for my brother.

slides.text: A Compound Sentence consists of two or more connected sentences, each of which will make complete sense when standing alone.
examples: Wheat grows in the field, **and** men reap it.
The wind blew, **but** the ship was safe.
He is at home, **or** he is at school.

slides.heading: Members & Common Parts
bullets: Rem. — The sentences of which a compound sentence is composed are called *Members*.
“Exercise strengthens the constitution, and temperance strengthens the constitution.” — *exercise* and *temperance* are the parts not common to the two members.

Rule. — A compound sentence containing common parts may be changed to a simple one by uniting the parts not common to all its members, and using the common parts but once:  “Exercise and temperance strengthen the constitution.”

slides.heading: Practice — Change to Simple
slides.instruction: Change each compound sentence to a simple one.
items: Behold my mother, and behold my brethren.
I saw a man in a boat, and I saw a boy in the water.
Washington was a warrior, and Washington was a statesman.
The man you saw was sick, or he was in trouble.
The river was swift, and it was very deep.
answers: Behold my mother and my brethren.
I saw a man in a boat and a boy in the water.
Washington was a warrior and a statesman.
The man you saw was sick or in trouble.  (one member now;  the clause *[whom] you saw* makes it complex)
The river was swift and very deep.

rows.sentence: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth his handiwork.
rows.note: Declarative; compound.  *The heavens declare the glory of God* is the first member;  *the firmament showeth his handiwork*, the second;  *and*, the connective.  *heavens* is the subject of the first member;  *declare*, the predicate.  *heavens* is modified by *The*, an adjective element;  *declare*, by *glory*, an objective element, which is modified by *the* and the phrase *of God*, adjective elements.  *firmament* is the subject of the second member;  *showeth* (= shows), the predicate.  *firmament* is modified by *the*, an adjective element;  *showeth*, by *handiwork*, an objective element, which is modified by *his*, an adjective element.

slides.heading: Practice — Members (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Name the members of each compound sentence and the connective.
items: Talent is something, but tact is every thing.
Art is long, and time is fleeting.
Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
The stores were closed, and the hum of business was hushed.
answers: Talent is something · tact is every thing — *but*
Art is long · time is fleeting — *and*
Lead us not into temptation · deliver us from evil — *but*
The stores were closed · the hum of business was hushed — *and*

slides.heading: Practice — Members (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Name the members of each compound sentence and the connective.
items: Every eye was filled with tears, and, for a moment, all were silent.
You may stay here with me, or we will go to the lecture with Susan.
The gathering clouds threatened an approaching storm, and the deep darkness of the night soon enveloped them.
answers: Every eye was filled with tears · for a moment, all were silent — *and*
You may stay here with me · we will go to the lecture with Susan — *or*
The gathering clouds threatened an approaching storm · the deep darkness of the night soon enveloped them — *and*

rows.sentence: Talent is something, but tact is every thing.
rows.note: Declarative; compound.  *Talent* is the subject of the first member;  *something*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  *tact* is the subject of the second;  *thing*, the predicate, modified by *every*, an adjective element;  *is*, the copula.  *but* is the connective.

rows.sentence: Art is long, and time is fleeting.
rows.note: Declarative; compound.  *Art* is the subject of the first member;  *long*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  *time* is the subject of the second;  *fleeting*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  *and* is the connective.  (*fleeting* = passing swiftly)

rows.sentence: Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
rows.note: Imperative; compound.  The subject of each member, *thou*, is understood.  *Lead* is the predicate of the first, modified by *us*, an objective element, and by *not* and the phrase *into temptation*, adverbial elements.  *deliver* is the predicate of the second, modified by *us*, an objective element, and by the phrase *from evil*, an adverbial element.  *but* is the connective.

rows.sentence: The gathering clouds threatened an approaching storm, and the deep darkness of the night soon enveloped them.
rows.note: Declarative; compound.  *clouds* is the subject of the first member;  *threatened*, the predicate.  *clouds* is modified by *The* and *gathering*, adjective elements;  *threatened*, by *storm*, an objective element, which *an* and *approaching* modify.  *darkness* is the subject of the second;  *enveloped*, the predicate.  *darkness* is modified by *the*, *deep*, and the phrase *of the night*, adjective elements;  *enveloped*, by *soon*, an adverbial element, and by *them*, an objective element.  *and* is the connective.

rows.sentence: The stores were closed, and the hum of business was hushed.
rows.note: Declarative; compound.  *stores* is the subject of the first member;  *were closed*, the predicate;  *stores* is modified by *The*, an adjective element.  *hum* is the subject of the second;  *was hushed*, the predicate;  *hum* is modified by *the* and the phrase *of business*, adjective elements.  *and* is the connective.

rows.sentence: Every eye was filled with tears, and, for a moment, all were silent.
rows.note: Declarative; compound.  *eye* is the subject of the first member;  *was filled*, the predicate.  *eye* is modified by *Every*, an adjective element;  *was filled*, by the phrase *with tears*, an adverbial element.  *all* is the subject of the second;  *silent*, the predicate;  *were*, the copula;  *silent* is modified by the phrase *for a moment*, an adverbial element.  *and* is the connective.

rows.sentence: You may stay here with me, or we will go to the lecture with Susan.
rows.note: Declarative; compound.  *You* is the subject of the first member;  *may stay*, the predicate, modified by *here* and the phrase *with me*, adverbial elements.  *we* is the subject of the second;  *will go*, the predicate, modified by the phrases *to the lecture* and *with Susan*, adverbial elements.  *or* is the connective.

slides.heading: Members & Truth
bullets: Each member of a declarative compound sentence is a proposition, true or false by itself.  (A command — *Lead us not…* — is neither.)
*and*, *but* — both members are affirmed:  true if both are true;  false if either is false.  *but* adds contrast, not a different truth.
*or* — true if at least one member is true;  false only if neither is.
*either…or* — true if exactly one member is true;  false if neither is, or both are.

slides.text: A Complex Sentence is one some element of which contains a subject and a predicate.
examples: The house **that Jack built** is old.

slides.heading: Principal & Subordinate Clauses
bullets: A sentence, any element of which is a clause, is a Complex Sentence.  A clause must contain a subject and a predicate.
“I know where gold is found.” — *I know* makes complete sense standing alone:  the *Principal Clause*.  *where gold is found* does not:  a *Subordinate Clause*.
A Principal Clause is one which makes complete sense when separated from the rest of the sentence.
A Subordinate Clause is one which does not make complete sense when separated from the rest of the sentence.

rows.label: Subject
rows.text: A clause used as the subject.
rows.examples: “**Haste makes waste**,” is a true saying.

rows.label: Predicate
rows.text: A clause used as the predicate.
rows.examples: My hope is, **that he will recover**.

rows.label: Objective
rows.text: A clause used as an objective element.
rows.examples: I believe **that the earth is round**.

rows.label: Adjective
rows.text: A clause used as an adjective element.
rows.examples: The report **that he is insane**, is unfounded.

rows.label: Adverbial
rows.text: A clause used as an adverbial element.
rows.examples: Our teacher is delighted **when we are studious**.

slides.heading: Remarks on Analysis
bullets: Rem. 1. — A complex sentence whose subject or predicate only is a clause need not be separated into principal and subordinate clauses in analysis.
Rem. 2. — Some complex sentences are composed of many clauses.  Each clause should be analyzed in the order indicated by its position.

rows.sentence: He that hateth, dissembleth with his lips.
rows.note: Declarative; complex;  composed of a principal clause and a subordinate clause.  *He dissembleth with his lips* is the principal clause;  *that hateth*, the subordinate clause.  *He* is the subject of the principal clause;  *dissembleth*, the predicate.  *He* is modified by the clause *that hateth*, an adjective element, of which *that* is the subject, and *hateth*, the predicate.  *dissembleth* is modified by the phrase *with his lips*, an adverbial element;  *lips*, by *his*, an adjective element.  (*hateth* = hates;  *dissembleth* = hides his true feelings)

rows.sentence: That he is very sick, is evident.
rows.note: Declarative; complex;  its subject is a clause, so it is not separated into principal and subordinate clauses (Rem. 1).  *That he is very sick* is the subject;  *evident*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  *he* is the subject of the subject clause;  *sick*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  *sick* is modified by *very*, an adverbial element.  *That* is a conjunction used to introduce the subject clause.

rows.sentence: He never denied that the letter was lost.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *He never denied* is the principal clause;  *the letter was lost*, the subordinate clause;  *that*, the connective.  *He* is the subject of the principal clause;  *denied*, the predicate, which is modified by *never*, an adverbial element, and by the clause *that the letter was lost*, an objective element.  *letter* is the subject of the subordinate clause;  *was lost*, the predicate;  *letter* is modified by *the*, an adjective element.  *that* joins the clause *the letter was lost* to *denied*.

rows.sentence: He builds a palace of ice where the torrents fall.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *He builds a palace of ice* is the principal clause;  *the torrents fall*, the subordinate clause;  *where*, the connective.  *He* is the subject of the principal clause;  *builds*, the predicate, which is modified by *palace*, an objective element, and by the clause *where the torrents fall*, an adverbial element.  *palace* is modified by *a* and the phrase *of ice*, adjective elements.  *torrents* is the subject of the subordinate clause;  *fall*, the predicate.  *torrents* is modified by *the*, an adjective element;  *fall*, by *where*, an adverbial element.

slides.heading: Clauses & Truth
bullets: A subordinate clause is a proposition used as an element:  it is not affirmed on its own, as a member is.
“He never denied that the letter was lost.” — true or false whether or not the letter was lost.
“That he is very sick, is evident.” — *evident* is affirmed of a whole proposition:  *he is very sick*.

slides.heading: Practice — Subordinate Clauses (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Name the subordinate clause and tell its class.
items: He that flattereth, deceiveth his neighbor.
The boy that you saw, is my younger brother.
He was frightened when he first saw a lion.
I can not study where pupils make so much noise.
answers: that flattereth — adjective
that you saw — adjective
when he first saw a lion — adverbial
where pupils make so much noise — adverbial

slides.heading: Practice — Subordinate Clauses (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Name the subordinate clause and tell its class.
items: I would pay you if I had the money.
That he will succeed, is uncertain.
The messenger reported that the brave general was dead.
He is a good man, though very eccentric.
answers: if I had the money — adverbial
That he will succeed — subject  (Rem. 1)
that the brave general was dead — objective
though [he is] very eccentric — adverbial

slides.heading: Practice — Subordinate Clauses (Set 3)
slides.instruction: Name every subordinate clause and tell its class.
items: Nature never did betray the heart that loved her.
The poor too often turn away, unheard, / From hearts that shut against them, with a sound / That shall be heard in heaven.  — Longfellow
answers: that loved her — adjective
that shut against them — adjective (modifies *hearts*);  That shall be heard in heaven — adjective (modifies *sound*)

rows.sentence: He that flattereth, deceiveth his neighbor.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *He deceiveth his neighbor* is the principal clause;  *that flattereth*, the subordinate clause.  *He* is the subject;  *deceiveth*, the predicate.  *He* is modified by the clause *that flattereth*, an adjective element, of which *that* is the subject, and *flattereth*, the predicate.  *deceiveth* is modified by *neighbor*, an objective element, which *his* modifies.  (*flattereth* = flatters;  *deceiveth* = deceives)

rows.sentence: The boy that you saw, is my younger brother.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *The boy is my younger brother* is the principal clause;  *that you saw*, the subordinate clause.  *boy* is the subject;  *brother*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  *boy* is modified by *The* and by the clause *that you saw*, adjective elements;  *brother*, by *my* and *younger*, adjective elements.  In the clause, *you* is the subject;  *saw*, the predicate, modified by *that*, an objective element.

rows.sentence: He was frightened when he first saw a lion.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *He was frightened* is the principal clause;  *he first saw a lion*, the subordinate clause;  *when*, the connective.  *He* is the subject;  *was frightened*, the predicate, modified by the clause *when he first saw a lion*, an adverbial element.  In the clause, *he* is the subject;  *saw*, the predicate, modified by *when* and *first*, adverbial elements, and by *lion*, an objective element, which *a* modifies.

rows.sentence: I can not study where pupils make so much noise.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *I can not study* is the principal clause;  *pupils make so much noise*, the subordinate clause;  *where*, the connective.  *I* is the subject;  *can study*, the predicate, modified by *not* and by the clause *where pupils make so much noise*, adverbial elements.  In the clause, *pupils* is the subject;  *make*, the predicate, modified by *where*, an adverbial element, and by *noise*, an objective element.  *noise* is modified by *much*, an adjective element;  *much*, by *so*, an adverbial element.

rows.sentence: I would pay you if I had the money.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *I would pay you* is the principal clause;  *I had the money*, the subordinate clause;  *if*, the connective.  *I* is the subject;  *would pay*, the predicate, modified by *you*, an objective element, and by the clause *if I had the money*, an adverbial element.  In the clause, *I* is the subject;  *had*, the predicate, modified by *money*, an objective element, which *the* modifies.

rows.sentence: That he will succeed, is uncertain.
rows.note: Declarative; complex;  its subject is a clause, so it is not separated into principal and subordinate clauses (Rem. 1).  *That he will succeed* is the subject;  *uncertain*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  In the subject clause, *he* is the subject;  *will succeed*, the predicate.  *That* is a conjunction introducing the clause.

rows.sentence: The messenger reported that the brave general was dead.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *The messenger reported* is the principal clause;  *the brave general was dead*, the subordinate clause;  *that*, the connective.  *messenger* is the subject;  *reported*, the predicate.  *messenger* is modified by *The*, an adjective element;  *reported*, by the clause *that the brave general was dead*, an objective element.  In the clause, *general* is the subject;  *dead*, the predicate;  *was*, the copula;  *general* is modified by *the* and *brave*, adjective elements.

rows.sentence: He is a good man, though very eccentric.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *He is a good man* is the principal clause;  *[he is] very eccentric*, the subordinate clause, its subject and copula understood;  *though*, the connective.  *He* is the subject;  *man*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  *man* is modified by *a* and *good*, adjective elements.  The clause *though very eccentric* is an adverbial element.  In it, *eccentric* is the predicate, modified by *very*, an adverbial element.

rows.sentence: Nature never did betray the heart that loved her.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *Nature never did betray the heart* is the principal clause;  *that loved her*, the subordinate clause.  *Nature* is the subject;  *did betray*, the predicate, modified by *never*, an adverbial element, and by *heart*, an objective element.  *heart* is modified by *the* and by the clause *that loved her*, adjective elements.  In the clause, *that* is the subject;  *loved*, the predicate, modified by *her*, an objective element.

rows.sentence: The poor too often turn away, unheard, / From hearts that shut against them, with a sound / That shall be heard in heaven.  — Longfellow

slides.heading: Complex Sentences (10) — Three Clauses
bullets: Declarative;  complex, of three clauses (Rem. 2).

Principal:  *The poor too often turn away, unheard, from hearts.*  *poor* (an adjective used as a noun) is the subject, modified by *The* and *unheard*;  *turn*, the predicate, modified by *often* (which *too* modifies), *away*, and *from hearts*.

Subordinate:  *that shut against them, with a sound* — an adjective element modifying *hearts*;  *that*, its subject;  *shut*, its predicate, modified by the phrases *against them* and *with a sound*.
Subordinate:  *That shall be heard in heaven* — an adjective element modifying *sound*;  *That*, its subject;  *shall be heard*, its predicate, modified by the phrase *in heaven*.

slides.heading: Reducing & Enlarging
bullets: Complex sentences may often be reduced to simple sentences by using single words or phrases, instead of subordinate propositions, as modifiers.
“A man who is wealthy, lives there” = “A man of wealth lives there,” or “A wealthy man lives there.”
Simple sentences may often be enlarged to complex sentences by using subordinate propositions, instead of single words or phrases, as modifiers.
“None think the great unhappy but the great” = “None think that the great are unhappy but the great.”

slides.heading: Practice — Reduce to Simple (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Reduce each complex sentence to a simple sentence.  Model — “We started when the sun rose” = “We started at sunrise.”
items: A pupil that is studious, will learn rapidly.
Men who are honest, are respected.
A boy, when he is at play, is happy.
An accident that was unavoidable, occurred at the factory this morning.
answers: A studious pupil will learn rapidly.
Honest men are respected.
A boy at play is happy.
An unavoidable accident occurred at the factory this morning.

slides.heading: Practice — Reduce to Simple (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Reduce each complex sentence to a simple sentence.
items: Franklin, who was a philosopher, was an American.
One soldier was not present when the roll was called.
They weighed anchor when the tide turned.  (*weighed anchor* = raised anchor to sail)
My brother has gone to the city that he may find employment.
answers: Franklin, a philosopher, was an American.
One soldier was not present at roll call.
They weighed anchor at the turn of the tide.
My brother has gone to the city to find employment.

slides.heading: Practice — Enlarge to Complex (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Enlarge each simple sentence to a complex sentence, using a clause instead of the marked words.
items: A thing **of beauty** is a joy forever.
I went down to the river **at ten o’clock**.
Thou hast uttered **cruel** words.
The poor must work **in their grief**.
answers: A thing that is beautiful is a joy forever.
I went down to the river when it was ten o’clock.
Thou hast uttered words that are cruel.
The poor must work while they grieve.

slides.heading: Practice — Enlarge to Complex (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Enlarge each simple sentence to a complex sentence, using a clause instead of the marked words.
items: Time **wasted** is existence;  **used**, is life.
They came here **to see the country**.
The wild beasts **kept for the games**, had broken from their dens.
Haste **to cheer my father’s heart**.  (*Haste* = hurry)
answers: Time that is wasted is existence;  time that is used is life.
They came here that they might see the country.
The wild beasts that were kept for the games, had broken from their dens.
Haste, that thou mayest cheer my father’s heart.

slides.heading: Practice — Which Kind?
slides.instruction: Name the kind of each sentence.
items: Iron and lead are heavy.
The sun rose, and the mist vanished.
The tree that fell was an oak.
We waited until noon.
We waited until he came.
He is poor, but he is honest.
He said that the road was closed.
Eli ran, jumped, and shouted.
answers: simple
compound
complex
simple
complex
compound
complex
simple

slides.heading: Oral Lesson — the Interjection
bullets: “Hurra! we have found him.” — *we* is the subject;  *have found*, the predicate, modified by *him*, an objective element.
What does *hurra* denote?  That the speaker or writer is highly pleased.  Does it affirm or deny any thing?  It does not:  it simply implies a feeling or emotion of pleasure.
Other words denote sorrow, grief, surprise, disgust, pity, hatred, etc.  All such words are called *Interjections*.

slides.text: An Interjection is a word used to denote some sudden or strong emotion.

slides.heading: Remarks on the Interjection
bullets: Rem. — Interjections usually, but not always, require an exclamation point [ ! ] after them.
An interjection is no part of the proposition:  “Alas! the ship was lost” is true just when the ship was lost.
Note. — Interjections may be omitted in analysis.  In a diagram they may be placed before and a little above the first words.

rows.sentence: Hurra! we have found him.
rows.note: Declarative; simple.  *we* is the subject;  *have found*, the predicate, modified by *him*, an objective element.  *Hurra* is an interjection;  it denotes that the speaker is highly pleased.

rows.sentence: Hush! they are coming.
rows.note: Declarative; simple.  *they* is the subject;  *are coming*, the predicate.  *Hush* is an interjection;  it denotes some sudden emotion.

slides.heading: Practice — Interjections (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Point out the interjection in each sentence.
items: Ha! it freezes me.
Aha! you are a truant.
Ahem! I will think about it.
Hark! the clock strikes one.
Pshaw! I knew that yesterday.
Alas! we shall see him no more.
answers: Ha
Aha
Ahem
Hark
Pshaw
Alas

slides.heading: Practice — Interjections (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Point out the interjections in each sentence.
items: Tush! tush! man, I made no reference to you.
Ay, he is every inch a king.
Oh, what a noble mind is here o’erthrown!  (*o’erthrown* = overthrown)
Alas! they had been friends in youth.
Hark! hark! the lark at heaven’s gate sings.
Alas! for the rarity of Christian charity.
answers: Tush, tush
Ay  (= yes)
Oh
Alas
Hark, hark
Alas

slides.heading: Practice — Parts of Speech (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Point out all the parts of speech in each sentence.
items: Ha! it freezes me.
Aha! you are a truant.
Alas! they had been friends in youth.
Alas! we shall see him no more.
answers: Ha — interjection;  it — pronoun;  freezes — verb;  me — pronoun
Aha — interjection;  you — pronoun;  are — verb;  a — adjective (article);  truant — noun
Alas — interjection;  they — pronoun;  had been — verb;  friends — noun;  in — preposition;  youth — noun
Alas — interjection;  we — pronoun;  shall see — verb;  him — pronoun;  more — adverb (modifies *shall see*);  no — adverb (modifies *more*)

slides.heading: Practice — Parts of Speech (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Point out all the parts of speech in each sentence.
items: Ahem! I will think about it.
Hark! hark! the lark at heaven’s gate sings.
Tush! tush! man, I made no reference to you.
Alas! for the rarity of Christian charity.
answers: Ahem — interjection;  I — pronoun;  will think — verb;  about — preposition;  it — pronoun
Hark, hark — interjections;  the — adjective (article);  lark — noun;  at — preposition;  heaven’s — noun (possessive);  gate — noun;  sings — verb
Tush, tush — interjections;  man — noun;  I — pronoun;  made — verb;  no — adjective;  reference — noun;  to — preposition;  you — pronoun
Alas — interjection;  for — preposition;  the — adjective (article);  rarity — noun;  of — preposition;  Christian — adjective;  charity — noun

slides.heading: Practice — Parts of Speech (Set 3)
slides.instruction: Point out all the parts of speech in each sentence.
items: Hark! the clock strikes one.
Pshaw! I knew that yesterday.
Ay, he is every inch a king.
Oh, what a noble mind is here o’erthrown!
answers: Hark — interjection;  the — adjective (article);  clock — noun;  strikes — verb;  one — noun (the hour)
Pshaw — interjection;  I — pronoun;  knew — verb;  that — pronoun;  yesterday — adverb
Ay — interjection;  he — pronoun;  is — verb;  every — adjective;  inch — noun;  a — adjective (article);  king — noun
Oh — interjection;  what — adjective;  a — adjective (article);  noble — adjective;  mind — noun;  is o’erthrown — verb;  here — adverb

slides.heading: The Eight Parts of Speech
bullets: Noun — a name.
Pronoun — used instead of a noun.
Verb — expresses action, being, or state.
Adjective — describes or defines a noun.
Adverb — modifies a verb, an adjective, a participle, or an adverb.
Preposition — shows the relation between its object and some other word.
Conjunction — connects words, phrases, clauses, and members.
Interjection — denotes some sudden or strong emotion.
